extracted.intended_audience: teachers and students of American history; students/scholars of public administration and political science
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and classroom use of Woodrow Wilson's 1887 essay 'The Study of Administration' as a primary-source statement of progressive-era administrative theory and practical criteria for organizing government administration in a democratic republic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between politics and administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Administration lies outside the proper sphere of politics; administrative questions are not political questions. Politics sets the tasks for administration but should not manipulate its offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilson (citing Bluntschli) emphasizes separating 'the activity of the state in things great and universal' (politics) from 'the activity of the state in individual and small things' (administration). This distinction underpins arguments about professionalizing and insulating administration from partisan manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between constitutional and administrative questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutional questions concern general law and principle; administrative questions concern the detailed, instrumental application and execution of those laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilson gives examples (tax assessment, hanging a criminal, mail delivery, military recruiting) to show that administration is the particular application of general law and thus outside the province of constitutional prescription, though administrative study may inform distribution of authority (a constitutional concern).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration as the detailed, systematic execution of public law
rubrics_metrics.description: Public administration is the detailed and systematic execution of public law; every particular application of general law is an act of administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion frames administration as technical, bureaucratic work (means rather than ends) and underlies calls for scientific and professional methods in administering government functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to clearly fix distribution of authority and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative organization must discover arrangements that unmistakably fix responsibility on officials and divide authority without hampering it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilson argues that clear assignment of responsibility is crucial to trustworthiness and accountability; administrative study should seek the simplest arrangements that enable this clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center power to enable accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Large powers and unhampered discretion centered in heads of service are indispensable conditions of responsibility because they make it easy to direct praise or blame to the right person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilson contends that dividing power into many small shares obscures responsibility and encourages remissness, whereas concentrated authority, paired with accountability, fosters conscientious performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion as authoritative critic, not daily manager
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion should play the role of authoritative critic over administration, exercising supervision of broad policy but not meddling in daily operational details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilson stresses making public criticism efficient without letting it become intrusive; public oversight is beneficial when it governs formative policy but is a 'clumsy nuisance' if it controls everyday means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make public opinion efficient through education and persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative improvement in a democracy requires educating and persuading the public to want particular reforms; reforms must be won by shaping public opinion over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because democracies contain diverse and often intransigent opinions, administrative reform is slow and must proceed by creating common understanding and demand among varied constituencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train and prepare competent officials (professional civil service)
rubrics_metrics.description: A technically schooled civil service, prepared by special schooling and competitive examinations, is indispensable to effective administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilson advocates sending candidates to civil service exams after technical preparation, establishing hierarchy and discipline, and drilling appointees into organized bureaucracies—while guarding against creation of an isolated official class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil service must be sensitive to public opinion (avoid officious class)
rubrics_metrics.description: A trained, tenure-protected civil service must remain intimately connected to popular thought so it does not become a divorced, officious official class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilson insists that 'good behavior' for officials means steady allegiance to the government's policy and that structures (elections, public counsel) should keep officials accountable and aligned with public values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance tenure and responsiveness (service during good behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: Officials serving 'during good behavior' (tenure protections) are a business necessity, but their conduct must be anchored to public opinion and responsibility to avoid un-American officialism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion supports protective tenure to secure expertise while requiring mechanisms that tie officials' advancement and accountability to public policy and opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative study must both educate critics and produce skilled administrators
rubrics_metrics.description: The science of administration has a dual duty: to instruct the public what administration to desire and how to get it, and to prepare competent, technically skilled administrative personnel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilson notes that political education (e.g., chairs of political science) increases intelligent critics but does not by itself create skilled executive officials; both cultivation and schooling are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative method: borrow foreign administrative techniques guardedly
rubrics_metrics.description: Studying foreign administrative systems is useful and safe if their methods are filtered through and adapted to American constitutional and political conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilson argues comparative study can supply practical methods without importing incompatible political systems, provided foreign practices are 'distilled' and 'Americanized' in thought and principle, not copied wholesale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Americanize administrative science for decentralized government
rubrics_metrics.description: The science of administration must be adapted to the United States' complex, multiform, highly decentralized constitutional system rather than the centralized models suited to European states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilson calls for radical, not merely linguistic, adaptation: learn the U.S. constitutions by heart, remove bureaucratic rigidities, and tailor techniques to local and federal divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intergovernmental cooperation with preserved autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to make town, city, county, state, and federal governments robust and cooperative while each keeps its own master; combine independence with mutual helpfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilson envisions federated systems 'within systems' that operate with like strength and healthfulness to serve common purposes without centralizing incompatible authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration as technical/scientific expertise applying means to political ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Administration concerns the application of bureaucratic, technical, and scientific expertise to the particular details or means of government rather than the broad ends of politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This characterization justifies professionalization, technical schooling, and the idea that administrative study is a distinct scientific field focused on efficiency, equity, speed, and reduced friction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy makes organizing administration harder
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular sovereignty complicates organizing administration because a multitudinous, diverse 'sovereign' requires education and persuasion rather than simple commands; reforms must be compromises responsive to many views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilson explains that unlike a single monarch, public opinion is plural and slow to change; administrative reform in democracies must accommodate differences in race, class, and background and proceed gradually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of responsibility fosters trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating conditions where responsibility is unmistakably fixed fosters trustfulness rather than suspicion, which is necessary for healthy administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilson links constitutional reformers' work to administrative organization: clear responsibilities, easy public scrutiny, and visible accountability are instruments to convert suspicion into trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give public criticism control over policy but shield technical administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Find institutional means to give public criticism authoritative control over formative policy decisions while preventing it from interfering with technical and daily administrative operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilson challenges administrative study to devise mechanisms that render public oversight effective where appropriate and that keep it from becoming 'meddlesome' in operational choices.
